tour.title: What This Portal Is
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what the SPO Admin Portal actually does: staff manage properties, maintenance requests, walkthrough inspections, assets, vendor contacts and invoices, while residents submit and track their own requests. The critical idea it introduces up front is that there are three kinds of user — admin, regional administrator and resident — and each sees a completely different set of pages. CLAUDE.md is the standing engineering context that expands on the same story with the invariants that keep this codebase honest, and the rest of the tour follows that request path through real code.

tour.title: Boot and Configuration
tour.description: This is a single Express server that serves both the REST API and the compiled React SPA on one port — there is no separate frontend server. server/index.ts is the entry point, and the ordering inside it matters: config.ts validates every required environment variable and reports the failures together before anything else loads, so a misconfigured deployment dies at boot instead of erroring on a random request an hour later. security.ts then installs the Helmet headers and production CSP plus the upload and webhook rate limits, and errors.ts supplies the classification layer that turns thrown values into safe responses.
tour.languageLesson: Fail-fast configuration is a TypeScript-friendly pattern: parse the environment once into a typed, frozen object at module load, and export that instead of reading process.env throughout the code. Everything downstream then gets a non-optional type rather than `string | undefined`, which removes a whole class of runtime null checks.

tour.title: The Route Surface
tour.description: Every API endpoint lives in one large file, server/routes.ts — roughly 55 handlers, 22 of which are modeled as their own nodes in this graph. It has by far the highest fan-out in the codebase because it is the junction where authorization, validation and persistence meet. Read a couple of representative handlers first: GET /api/auth/user is what the frontend calls to learn who is signed in (it returns the database user plus permissions, deliberately not raw identity-provider claims), while GET /api/properties and GET /api/maintenance-requests show the standard shape every data route follows.
tour.languageLesson: Handlers parse request bodies with the Zod insert schemas generated from the Drizzle tables — `insertXSchema.parse(...)` for POST, `.partial().parse(...)` for PATCH. Zod validates and narrows the type in one step, so after the parse call the body is statically typed rather than `any`, and untrusted `req.body` never reaches the storage layer directly.

tour.title: Authorization, Layer by Layer
tour.description: This is the single most error-prone area in the codebase, so read it slowly. Three layers apply to every data route: authenticated (the isAuthenticated middleware from auth.ts), active (currentUser.isActive must be true), and permitted — either the user is an admin, or their user_permissions row grants the relevant flag. The trap is that admins frequently have no user_permissions row at all, so any check that only reads that row locks admins out; always compute isAdmin and bypass with it, which the helpers in authz.ts do for you. Region scoping lives here too, and filterByRegion deliberately returns an empty array when allowedRegions is empty — no regions means no access, not all access.
tour.languageLesson: Note the `requireActiveUser(req, res)` shape: it returns a context object or `null` after having already written the error response, so call sites read `const ctx = await requireActiveUser(req, res); if (!ctx) return;`. That narrowing idiom lets one helper own both the check and the refusal while TypeScript still proves `ctx` is defined below the guard.

tour.title: The Storage Seam
tour.description: Route handlers never touch the database directly — every query goes through the single IStorage interface exported as `storage` from server/storage.ts. This is an enforced seam rather than a stylistic preference: it is the only reason the data layer is testable and swappable, and it is why the authorization tests can exercise real HTTP routes without a database. db.ts sits underneath it with Drizzle over a standard pg pool. One piece of storage.ts deserves special attention: upsertUser contains email-based account re-linking, which is what lets an admin pre-create an account before somebody's first login and what makes swapping identity providers survivable.
tour.languageLesson: Exporting an interface (`IStorage`) alongside a single concrete instance (`storage`) is the TypeScript form of the repository pattern. Because the interface is the import target, a test can substitute a stub and the compiler will flag any method the stub forgot — the seam is checked at build time, not just by convention.

tour.title: The Single Source of Truth
tour.description: shared/schema.ts is the highest fan-in file in the whole project — 46 modules depend on it, on both sides of the wire. It defines the fifteen tables with Drizzle and generates matching Zod insert schemas with drizzle-zod, so the server's query types, the client's response types and the form validation rules all derive from one file. drizzle.config.ts tells drizzle-kit where that schema lives and where to emit migrations. Because a single edit here ripples into both the API and the React forms, schema changes always ship with a generated migration in the same change.
tour.languageLesson: Drizzle infers TypeScript types straight from the table definitions, so there is no separate type declaration to keep in sync — `typeof users.$inferSelect` is the row type. drizzle-zod then derives a runtime validator from the same definition, which is how one file can be simultaneously the database schema, the compile-time type and the request validator.

tour.title: Tables and Migrations
tour.description: The migrations directory is the reproducible history of the schema you just read. The baseline migration records the tables that predate the migrations folder, and each numbered file after it adds one thing — uploads, the audit log, property chapters, maintenance schedules, residents, resident finances. Four tables carry most of the domain: users holds accounts keyed by the identity provider's subject claim, user_permissions holds one row per user with thirteen boolean flags plus allowedRegions, maintenance_requests is the core workflow, and properties is what regional scoping filters against. The journal file is what drizzle-kit reads to know which migrations have been applied.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations must be ordered and append-only: once a numbered file has run anywhere, you add a new one rather than editing it. `npm run db:push` writes the schema straight to a database without leaving a migration behind, which is fine for throwaway experiments but leaves no record of how to reproduce the result — anything reaching production has to be a committed migration.

tour.title: File Uploads, Both Directions
tour.description: All file storage goes through one FileStore interface in server/objectStorage/, with a local folder driver for development and a private Supabase bucket for production, selected by STORAGE_DRIVER — nothing else in the app talks to a bucket. Writing is guarded twice over: uploadLimits.ts reserves in-flight byte capacity from Content-Length before the body is read (a burst degrades into a 503 retry rather than an out-of-memory crash), and POST /api/upload validates the extension, the MIME type and the file's actual magic bytes, so a renamed executable is rejected before anything is stored. Reading back is the subtler half: GET /uploads/:filename is authenticated, not express.static, and it checks existence only after authorizing so a refusal cannot confirm which filenames are real.
tour.languageLesson: The permission check must sit *before* the multer middleware in the handler chain. Express middleware runs in registration order, so a guard placed after the parser means a caller with no right to upload still gets their entire request body read into memory — ordering is a security property here, not a style choice.

tour.title: The Audit Trail
tour.description: server/audit.ts records the actions somebody may have to account for later: user and permission changes, maintenance status changes, invoice and billing changes, and document uploads and downloads. Two properties are load-bearing. It never fails a request — recordAuditEvent returns immediately and swallows both synchronous throws and rejected writes, because deactivating an account must not error just because the log was unreachable. And it never stores a credential: callers pass details field by field rather than handing over a request body, and scrubDetails redacts any key whose name looks like a secret or banking identifier. shared/audit.ts holds AUDIT_ACTIONS, the closed vocabulary you extend rather than passing a bare string.
tour.languageLesson: AUDIT_ACTIONS is declared with `as const`, which turns the array into a readonly tuple of string literals so a union type can be derived from it. That is what makes a typo in an action name a compile error instead of a silently unqueryable row in an append-only table.

tour.title: Webhooks and Scheduled Work
tour.description: Two things happen without a signed-in user driving them. The JotForm webhook turns form submissions into maintenance requests, and it fails closed: with no JOTFORM_WEBHOOK_SECRET configured it returns 503 rather than accepting anonymous submissions, and the secret is compared in constant time. Its companion config endpoint exposes the current field mapping to the admin setup dialog. Separately, schedules.ts runs the daily jobs — most notably audit retention, which keeps routine events for two years while retaining account and permission events indefinitely, deleting at most 1,000 rows per pass so one large statement never locks the table.
tour.languageLesson: Constant-time secret comparison exists because a normal `===` on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, leaking the length of the matching prefix through response timing. Any comparison of an attacker-supplied value against a secret should use a fixed-time helper — here, `secretsMatch()`.

tour.title: The React Entry and Role Routing
tour.description: Now cross to the other side of the wire. main.tsx mounts the app, and App.tsx does something unusual: routing is Wouter, and it is role-based — App.tsx renders a completely different <Switch> depending on whether the signed-in user is an admin or regional administrator versus a resident. There is no per-route guard, because unauthenticated visitors only ever reach the Landing page. useAuth.ts is the hook that supplies the user object every one of those decisions reads, populated from the GET /api/auth/user endpoint you saw in Step 3.
tour.languageLesson: React's rules of hooks bite hard here: never put an early return between hook calls. A guard like `if (!isAdmin) return <AccessDenied />` placed above a `useQuery` changes the hook count once the auth query resolves, and React throws. Compute the guard from hooks, then return below all of them — this crashed the Settings page once already.

tour.title: Client Data and Cache Invalidation
tour.description: Server state is TanStack Query, configured in lib/queryClient.ts with staleTime: Infinity, no refetch on focus and no retries. That configuration is a deliberate trade and it hands you one obligation: you must invalidate the relevant query keys manually after every mutation, or the UI will keep showing stale data indefinitely. The default query function derives the URL by joining the query key with a slash, so queryKey ['/api/assets'] fetches /api/assets, and apiRequest(method, url, data) is the mutation helper that throws on non-2xx. The Maintenance page and its edit dialog are the clearest worked example of the read-mutate-invalidate cycle end to end.
tour.languageLesson: TanStack Query treats the query key as both cache identity and cache-invalidation prefix, so `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['/api/maintenance-requests'] })` also clears keys nested beneath it. With staleTime set to Infinity nothing else will ever trigger a refetch, which is why the invalidation call is not optional cleanup — it is the only refresh mechanism the app has.

tour.title: The Shared UI Kit
tour.description: The pages you just read are thin because the repeated pieces are factored out, and these files have the highest fan-in on the client side. layout/page.tsx gives every page its consistent frame, states.tsx supplies the loading, empty and error states that 20 modules render, data-table.tsx handles list views, and format.ts holds formatDate and formatDateTime — dates are formatted at the render boundary, never earlier. Beneath these sit 22 generated shadcn/ui primitives in components/ui/; treat those as generated output and build new things in components/ instead of editing them.
tour.languageLesson: Path aliases keep these imports short and refactor-safe: `@/` maps to client/src/, `@shared/` to shared/, `@assets/` to attached_assets/. They are declared twice — in tsconfig.json for the type checker and in vite.config.ts for the bundler — and both must agree or the build and the editor will disagree about what resolves.

tour.title: The Safety Net
tour.description: The test suite is deliberately weighted towards authorization, because that is where a silent mistake costs the most. authz.test.ts exercises the rules on their own; routeAccess.test.ts exercises the same rules over real HTTP through the real login guard, which is what keeps the two historic guard gaps closed. Three conventions in that suite each exist because of a real miss: never re-implement the code under test inside the test, assert that the refused work never happened (a 403 alone does not prove the check ran before the write), and pair every 'was not called' assertion with a positive control so a typo cannot make it vacuous. CI runs lint, check, test and build on every push, and the e2e workflow drives the real browser on top.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows key off `on` triggers, run `jobs` in parallel and `steps` in sequence. The gate here is the same four commands you run locally — `npm run lint && npm run check && npm test && npm run build` — which is the point: CI should be a rerun of a check you can reproduce on your own machine, not a separate set of rules.
